scenes.caption: Photo 1900
scenes.text: The prayer hall, measuring about 26 by 50 metres (85 by 164 ft), occupies the eastern half of the mosque behind the qibla wall.

scenes.caption: Photo 1900
scenes.text: The actual date of construction of the first mosque in Djenné is unknown, but dates as early as 1200 and as late as 1330 have been suggested.

scenes.caption: Photo 1900
scenes.text: With the Moroccan invasion at the end of the 16th century the Songhay mosque was again destroyed and "that of Tanapo rebuilt." This was the mosque referred to in the Tarikh al-Sudan, the ruins of which were later observed and…

scenes.caption: Photo 1906
scenes.text: Between 1834 and 1836, Seku Amadu built a new mosque to the east of the existing one on the site of the former palace.

scenes.caption: Photo 1906
scenes.text: In 1906, the town arranged for the original mosque to be rebuilt and for a school to be constructed on the site of Seku Amadu's mosque.

scenes.caption: Photo 1906
scenes.text: The rebuilding was completed in 1907 using forced labour under the direction of Ismaila Traoré, head of Djenné's guild of masons.

scenes.caption: Photo 1909
scenes.text: In 1930, an inexact replica of the mosque was built in the town of Fréjus in southern France.

scenes.caption: Photo 1911
scenes.text: Along with the "Old Towns of Djenné", it was designated a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 1988.

scenes.caption: Photo 1931
scenes.text: The mosque is seen in the 2005 film Sahara.

scenes.title: The place
scenes.text: The largest mud-brick building in the world, rebuilt in 1907 on the site of a 13th-century mosque. Every year the whole town replasters its banco walls. UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1988.
